evidence_quotes.quote:
Survey data collected from participants in the Ahmedabad Slum Networking Project
(SNP) is analysed to examine the importance of community participation in
explaining respondent complaints about the project overall and with the specific
public services provided.

In other
words, perceived satisfaction of services
may only partially capture actual quality of
service provision.

Of the four variables included in this
model, only attend is statistically significant.

These results
suggest that respondents who are members
of CBOs with a close partnering relationship
with their sponsoring NGO, and/or have the
ability to communicate their needs to either
that NGO or to the municipality, are less
likely to have complained about the quality
or quantity of their water services.

As in the water services model,
respondents who report that their CBO has
frequently contacted their sponsoring NGO
to request service assistance (ngo_com) are
less likely to make negative comments about
their sewerage services than respondents who
do not report that their CBO is in frequent
contact with the sponsoring NGO.

findings.exact_estimate: Adjusted logistic regression: Odds Ratio (OR) = 1.44, S.E. = 0.28, statistically non-significant (p >= 0.05; no significance asterisks), N = 277; Model LR chi2(7) = 49.01 (p < 0.001), Pseudo R2 = 0.168 (Table 6, PDF p. 13 / journal p. 702). Note: In the sewerage complaints model (N = 300), attend was excluded (—) because it was not statistically significant in bivariate screening (PDF p. 11 / p. 700).

raw_response.headline_result_summary: In cross-sectional logistic regressions of 300 community-based organisation (CBO) leaders and members across 38 upgraded neighbourhoods in the Ahmedabad Slum Networking Project (SNP), the relationship between participatory governance and water/sanitation outcomes is mixed across mechanisms and outcomes (and relies on subjective satisfaction and open-ended service complaints rather than audited physical access). Sustained internal CBO participation (meeting attendance, attend) increases odds of rating overall multi-sector SNP quality as 'Very Satisfactory' (OR = 2.27, p < 0.001, N = 298), but is statistically null for complaints about poor water quality/quantity (OR = 1.44, SE = 0.28, p >= 0.05, N = 277) and excluded due to bivariate non-significance for sewerage complaints (N = 300). Conversely, external institutional redress and NGO linkage variables—specifically CBO frequency of contacting the sponsoring NGO (ngo_com: water OR = 0.56, p < 0.05; sewerage OR = 0.50, p < 0.01), CBO–NGO programme evaluation partnership (ngo_evl2: water OR = 0.15, p < 0.05), and CBO frequency of contacting the municipality (amc_com: water OR = 0.60, p < 0.05)—are associated with significantly lower odds of complaining about water and/or sewerage services, whereas municipal contact is null for sewerage complaints (OR = 1.56, SE = 0.42) and NGO decision dominance (d_ngo) and NGO-rated CBO activity (active3) are null/excluded for both water and sewerage.
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Outcome polarity inversion & Odds Ratio (< 1 vs. > 1) trap: In Table 6 (p. 702), Model 1 predicts a positive valence outcome (overall SNP quality is 'Very Satisfactory', OR > 1 = higher satisfaction), whereas Models 2–4 predict negative valence outcomes (complaining about poor quality or quantity of water, sewerage, or street lighting, so OR < 1 = negative log-odds = FEWER complaints / more favorable service perception, and OR > 1 = MORE complaints). Moreover, Table 6 prints Odds Ratios rather than log-odds coefficients; a careless coder could mistake OR = 0.56*, 0.60*, 0.15*, or 0.50** for positive coefficients or fail to invert complaint polarity. 2. Divergence between internal participation and external institutional linkages: The title's focal variable—sustained resident participation via CBO meeting attendance (attend)—is null for water complaints (OR = 1.44, SE = 0.28) and bivariate-insignificant/omitted for sewerage complaints, being significant only for composite SNP satisfaction (OR = 2.27***). By contrast, external NGO/municipal contact variables reduce water and (for NGO contact) sewerage complaints, while municipal contact is null for sewerage (OR = 1.56) and sharply increases street lighting complaints (amccntct OR = 8.33*). 3. Subjective complaining vs. physical household access: All sampled neighbourhoods had already received SNP physical upgrading and CBO registration for >= 3 years; there is no non-SNP control group and no physical measurement of water/sanitation connections, continuity, quality, or affordability. The authors explicitly caution (pp. 695, 699, 705) that professed satisfaction and open-ended complaining reflect social desirability and redress agency and only partially capture physical service quality. 4. Bivariate pre-screening omissions & PDF minus-sign glitch: Independent variables were retained in Table 6 only if bivariate-significant and r < 0.4 (p. 700), so '—' cells denote variables dropped for non-significance/collinearity. Also, in Table 6's PDF text layer, negative log-likelihood minus signs render as '2' ('2150.99' for –150.99, etc.; true negative values are confirmed in text on pp. 700, 703, 704). Mentioned 2SLS IV checks are not tabulated.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional stratified random survey (January–June 2009) analyzed with multivariate logistic regression (with untabulated 2SLS instrumental-variable robustness checks noted as yielding similar results)
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Individual community-based organisation (CBO) leaders and members across 38 SNP-registered, NGO-affiliated upgraded slum neighbourhoods in Ahmedabad (320 sampled from ~500 leaders/members in 38 of 52 eligible CBOs; N = 300 completed surveys; analytic N = 298 for overall SNP satisfaction, N = 277 for water complaints, N = 300 for sewerage complaints, N = 300 for street lighting complaints).
